study.title: Ranks and the process group
study.locator: Minutes 5:15 to 5:20: what torchrun assigns as global and local rank and why a process group is created

focus: Global rank \(r\) with \(0 \le r < W\) names one process in a run of \(W\) processes. Local rank names the same process inside its node. World size \(W\) is the process count, not the GPU count.
`RANK`, `WORLD_SIZE` and `LOCAL_RANK` come from the launcher. `MASTER_ADDR` and `MASTER_PORT` tell every process where rank 0 waits for the handshake.
Plan one process per GPU and set the device from the local rank, as in `torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)`. Two ranks sharing one GPU serialize kernels and break the one-device-per-rank NCCL setup.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, map 2 nodes with 4 GPUs each under one launcher job of 8 processes: the world size, the global ranks on each node, each rank's local rank, and the device each rank sets. Then state which rank holds local rank value 1 on the second node.
traps: Reading local rank as global rank on the second node. Local ranks restart at 0 on each node.
Launching more processes than GPUs and assigning two ranks to one device. NCCL expects one device per rank.
Setting WORLD_SIZE to a value that disagrees with the spawned process count. The init handshake waits for processes that never arrive.

selfTest.q: Two nodes hold 4 GPUs each and one job launches 8 processes. Which global ranks sit on node 1, and what is the local rank of global rank 6?
selfTest.a: Node 1 holds global ranks 4 to 7. Rank 6 has local rank 2 and uses the third GPU of that node.

selfTest.q: What does dist.init_process_group exchange between processes?
selfTest.a: Only handshake locations through the master address and port, a shared file, or a TCP endpoint. No tensors move; setup only makes later communication possible.

selfTest.q: A snippet calls dist.all_reduce(tensor, dst=0). Why is that wrong?
selfTest.a: dist.all_reduce takes no dst argument, and every rank keeps the reduced result. The dst argument belongs to dist.reduce, whose result is valid only on the root.

selfTest.q: Two ranks share one GPU and both call NCCL collectives. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The one-device-per-rank setup breaks. Kernels from both ranks serialize on the shared device, and the communicator is built per device, so sharing is unsupported even when it appears to start.

study.title: Steps 1 to 3 with diffs and the Part 1 video
study.locator: step2_process_group_manager and step3_dataloader with their diffs and the Part 1 video on the model, the process group manager and the dataloader
study.depth: Rebuild the rank grid yourself before reading the solution.

focus: A store is a key-value handshake, either `TCPStore` or `FileStore`. The launcher starts the processes, rendezvous introduces them, and `dist.init_process_group` builds the world group.
The default group holds all \(W\) ranks. `dist.new_group` carves named subsets, one rank may belong to several groups at once, and each group orders its own collectives.
Picotron lays ranks out as `torch.arange(world).view(dp, pp, cp, tp)` and enumerates one subgroup per axis. Every rank must build the identical grid or the groups disagree silently.
File init needs a nonexistent or empty shared file with fcntl locking. Mesh shapes must match on all ranks or setup hangs.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, take world size 4 with dp 2 and tp 2 in Picotron axis order: write the tensor-parallel groups and the data-parallel groups as rank sets.
traps: Reusing one fixed MASTER_PORT for several concurrent runs. The second job fails or joins the wrong rendezvous, so use a distinct port per run.
Trusting a LOCAL_RANK fallback of the form `global_rank % world_size` in example code on multiple nodes. It is not the true node-local rank.
Assuming subgroups inherit a barrier or an ordering from the world group. Each group needs its own calls in the same order.

selfTest.q: What does the store do, and when is it no longer needed?
selfTest.a: It exchanges handshake locations so ranks can find each other during init. After the process group is built, collectives use direct links and no longer consult the store.

selfTest.q: World size 4 with dp 2 and tp 2 in Picotron order: which ranks share a tensor-parallel group, and which share a data-parallel group?
selfTest.a: Tensor-parallel groups are {0, 1} and {2, 3}. Data-parallel groups are {0, 2} and {1, 3}.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 of a subgroup calls all_reduce but rank 1 of the same subgroup calls broadcast. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. Every member of a group must issue the same collective sequence, and subgroups do not inherit ordering from the world group.

selfTest.q: Two jobs on one machine share MASTER_PORT. What goes wrong?
selfTest.a: The second job either fails to bind or rendezvous with the wrong peers. Give each run its own port.

study.title: Send, receive and pipeline handoffs
study.locator: Minutes 7:08 to 7:10: send and receive as point-to-point primitives, with the pipeline send at minutes 9:59 to 10:00 as the use case

focus: Every `dist.send` names a dst and every `dist.recv` names a src, with a preallocated buffer of matching shape and dtype on the receiving rank. Blocking calls return after completion; immediates return a `Work` handle that requires `req.wait()`.
After `dist.isend`, writing the sent tensor is undefined until wait. After `dist.irecv`, reading the receive buffer is undefined until wait. After wait, the transfer is guaranteed.
Broadcast copies one source tensor to all ranks. Reduce combines every rank into dst only, so other ranks hold stale data after the call.
A send with no matching receive, or a receive with no send, blocks forever. The matched pair is the unit that must agree.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two-process exchange: rank 0 builds a 3-element tensor and sends it to rank 1 with isend and irecv plus wait, then rank 1 broadcasts it back so both ranks hold it. State every buffer each rank allocates.
traps: Allocating the receive buffer with the wrong shape or dtype. The call may hang or corrupt instead of raising.
Reading a reduce result on a non-root rank. Only dst holds the combined value.
Reusing a send buffer right after isend without wait. The transfer may still be in flight.

selfTest.q: What is the observable difference between dist.send with dist.recv and dist.isend with dist.irecv?
selfTest.a: The blocking pair returns after the transfer completes. The immediate pair returns a Work handle at once, and the transfer is only guaranteed after req.wait().

selfTest.q: Rank 0 calls isend on a tensor, then overwrites the tensor before wait. Rank 1 receives after its own wait. What can rank 1 hold?
selfTest.a: Anything, including a mix of old and new values. Writing a sent buffer before wait is undefined behaviour.

selfTest.q: Four ranks call dist.reduce with dst 0 and SUM. Afterwards rank 2 reads its tensor. What does it see?
selfTest.a: Its own stale input. Only rank 0 holds the combined sum after a reduce.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 sends to rank 1, but rank 1 never posts a receive and instead calls all_reduce. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. The send waits for a matching receive that never comes, and rank 1 waits at a collective rank 0 never joins.
